events.title: Accession of Nerva
events.summary: On the day of Domitian's murder the Senate recognised Marcus Cocceius Nerva, a 65-year-old jurist-senator of no military reputation who had served Nero and the Flavians, as emperor. He swore never to execute a senator, recalled exiles and punished informers.
events.detail: Tacitus praised him for having joined two things once incompatible, principate and liberty. An agrarian law and 60 million sesterces were spent buying land for poor citizens; the abuses of the fiscus Judaicus were curbed. But the leniency led the consul Fronto to remark that it was bad to have an emperor under whom nobody was allowed to do anything, but worse to have one under whom everybody could do everything. At a dinner Junius Mauricus, asked what the dead informer Catullus Messalinus would be doing if alive, answered 'dining with us'.
scholarship: Grainger, Nerva and the Roman Succession Crisis of AD 96-99 (2003)

events.title: Praetorian revolt and Nerva's adoption of Trajan
events.summary: In 97 the praetorians under their prefect Casperius Aelianus besieged the palace and forced Nerva to surrender Domitian's assassins for execution and even to thank the soldiers publicly. Weeks later, in the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol, Nerva announced the adoption of Marcus Ulpius Traianus, governor of upper Germany.
events.detail: Nerva had reportedly bared his throat to the mutineers. The choice of Trajan, a Spanish-born general from Italica with strong support among the armies, defused the crisis. Pliny's Panegyricus presents the adoption as the choice of the best man by divine guidance, the founding ideology of the 'adoptive emperors' (actually all, until Marcus, men without sons). The news arrived together with a laurelled dispatch announcing victory in Pannonia.

events.title: Death of Nerva; Trajan becomes emperor
events.summary: Nerva died of a fever after a fit of anger. Trajan, at Cologne, received the news from his cousin and ward Hadrian, who raced to deliver it, and became emperor without challenge; he did not return to Rome until 99, first inspecting the Rhine and Danube armies.
events.detail: Trajan had Casperius Aelianus and the mutinous praetorians summoned and executed. His entry into Rome on foot, embracing senators, is celebrated in the Panegyricus. He was the first emperor of provincial origin, from a colonist family of Italica in Baetica.

events.title: Tacitus's historical works
events.summary: Publius Cornelius Tacitus published the Agricola and Germania in 98, the Dialogus on orators around 102, the Histories (from 69 to 96) around 105-110, and the Annals (from 14 to 68) in the 110s-120s, the summit of Roman historiography.
events.detail: Less than half survives: the Histories break off in 70 and the Annals lack books 7-10 and parts of 5, 6, 11 and 16, all depending on two Medicean manuscripts. Tacitus's compressed style, irony and psychological insight shaped the modern image of the Julio-Claudians. His sources include the acta senatus (confirmed by the SC de Pisone patre), memoirs (Agrippina, Corbulo), and earlier histories (Aufidius Bassus, Pliny the Elder, Cluvius Rufus, Fabius Rusticus). The Germania, rediscovered in the Codex Hersfeldensis and exploited by German nationalists and the Nazis, became, in Christopher Krebs's phrase, 'a most dangerous book'.
scholarship: Syme, Tacitus (1958)
Krebs, A Most Dangerous Book (2011)

events.title: The Trajanic alimenta
events.summary: Building on a scheme begun by Nerva, Trajan established the alimenta in Italian towns: perpetual loans to local landowners at about 5% interest, secured on their estates, with the interest paying monthly allowances to support freeborn children.
events.detail: Two bronze tablets document it. The table of the Ligures Baebiani (101, CIL IX 1455) and the great table of Veleia near Piacenza (CIL XI 1147), the largest surviving Roman bronze inscription, record 1,044,000 sesterces lent to 52 landowners, supporting 263 boys at 16 sesterces a month, 35 girls at 12, and two illegitimate children. The arch of Beneventum and coins with ALIM(enta) ITAL(iae) celebrate it. Pliny implies a demographic and military purpose (future soldiers); others see charity or imperial display; the old theory of agricultural credit has been largely abandoned.
scholarship: Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (2nd ed. 1982), ch. 7
Woolf, 'Food, poverty and patronage', PBSR 58 (1990)

events.title: Battle of Tapae (101)
events.summary: Trajan's army fought Decebalus near Tapae, the gateway to the Dacian heartland, in a hard-won Roman victory amid a violent storm. The wounded were so many that Trajan tore up his own clothing for bandages and ordered an altar and annual rites for the fallen.
events.detail: Trajan's Column shows Jupiter hurling thunderbolts at the Dacians during the battle (scene XXIV). Before it, the Buri sent a message written in Latin on a giant mushroom urging Trajan to turn back (Dio 68.8.1). Despite victory the season was too far advanced to take Sarmizegetusa, and Trajan withdrew to winter quarters.

battle.significance: Opened the road into Dacia but at high cost.

events.title: Battle in Lower Moesia (Adamclisi)
events.summary: In winter 101/102 Dacians and Roxolani crossed the lower Danube into Moesia. Trajan hurried east by ship and defeated them in a series of fights, commemorated by the foundation of Nicopolis ad Istrum and, at Adamclisi in the Dobruja, by the colossal Tropaeum Traiani dedicated to Mars Ultor in 109.
events.detail: Column scenes XXXI-XLVII show Sarmatian cataphracts drowning in the Danube and a night battle. Beside the Tropaeum stands a mausoleum and a funerary altar inscribed with the names of some 3,800 soldiers who fell 'fighting for the state', probably in this campaign, though some attribute it to Fuscus's defeat of 86/87. The 54 metopes of the Tropaeum, carved in a provincial style, depict Roman and barbarian soldiers with unusual realism.

sides.strength: Imperial army including praetorians and Moorish cavalry
sides.losses: c. 3,800 named on the Adamclisi altar (if this battle)

battle.significance: Defeated the Dacian diversion and set up the decisive 102 campaign.

scholarship: Florescu, Das Siegesdenkmal von Adamklissi (1965)
Rossi, Trajan's Column and the Dacian Wars (1971)
events.debate: Location of the battle (Adamclisi vs Nicopolis ad Istrum) and the date of the altar.

events.title: Peace of 102
events.summary: As Roman columns stormed the forts of the Orăștie mountains, Decebalus submitted. He surrendered his arms, engines, engineers and deserters, agreed to demolish his forts, withdrew from conquered territory and accepted Rome's friends and enemies as his own; a Roman garrison stayed in Sarmizegetusa.
events.detail: The standard lost by Fuscus was recovered. Trajan took the title Dacicus and triumphed in December 102. Decebalus's envoys addressed the Senate with chained hands. The southern Banat and Oltenia stayed under Roman occupation, preparing the ground for the next war.

events.title: Trajan's bridge over the Danube
events.summary: Apollodorus of Damascus built a permanent bridge over the Danube between Drobeta and Pontes, about 1,135 m long, on twenty stone piers carrying timber arches, the longest arch bridge in the world for a millennium.
events.detail: Dio describes piers 150 feet high and 60 wide set 170 feet apart, founded in a deep, fast river, and calls it the most magnificent of Trajan's works. It appears on Trajan's Column and on coins. Hadrian removed the superstructure to prevent barbarians using it. Stumps of the piers survive on both banks. Upstream in the Iron Gates gorge, the Tabula Traiana inscription (100) records the cutting of a towpath road into the cliff.

events.title: Siege of Sarmizegetusa Regia
events.summary: In summer 106 Roman armies converged on Decebalus's mountain capital and religious centre, Sarmizegetusa Regia, cut its water supply and stormed it. Trajan's Column shows Dacian nobles taking poison from a cauldron rather than surrender, and the city set on fire.
events.detail: The site, at 1,200 m in the Orăștie mountains, contains a fortified hill, a sacred precinct with circular and rectangular sanctuaries and an andesite 'sun disc'. After capture a legionary detachment was stationed there and the sanctuaries were dismantled. Decebalus escaped with a few followers.

sides.strength: Several armies converging, perhaps 100,000 in the theatre

events.title: Death of Decebalus
events.summary: Pursued by Roman cavalry, Decebalus cut his own throat. The scout Tiberius Claudius Maximus reached him as he died, cut off his head and right hand and brought them to Trajan at Ranisstorum; the head was displayed on the Gemonian stairs in Rome.
events.detail: Maximus's tombstone, found in 1965 at Grammeni near Philippi, narrates his career and shows him galloping towards the falling king, matching Column scene CXLV. The Dacian noble Bicilis betrayed the treasure Decebalus had buried under the diverted river Sargetia. The king became a Romanian national hero in the modern period.
scholarship: Speidel, 'The captor of Decebalus', JRS 60 (1970)

events.title: Annexation of Nabataea as the province of Arabia
events.summary: On the death of the Nabataean king Rabbel II, the governor of Syria, Aulus Cornelius Palma, annexed the kingdom, apparently without serious fighting; the new province of Arabia, with its capital at Bostra and legio III Cyrenaica, dated its era from 22 March 106.
events.detail: Coins proclaim ARABIA ADQVISITA ('acquired'), not 'captured'. The Via Nova Traiana from Bostra to Aila on the Red Sea, completed 111-114, carried milestones stating that Trajan 'reduced Arabia to the form of a province and opened and paved a new road from the borders of Syria to the Red Sea'. The Babatha archive from the Cave of Letters shows Roman law and administration operating in the new province within a generation. Petra continued to flourish.
scholarship: Bowersock, Roman Arabia (1983)

events.title: Creation of the province of Dacia
events.summary: The conquered kingdom became the province of Dacia under a consular legate, garrisoned by legio XIII Gemina at Apulum and auxiliaries. Decimus Terentius Scaurianus founded Colonia Ulpia Traiana Augusta Dacica Sarmizegetusa for veterans, and settlers came 'from the whole Roman world'.
events.detail: Eutropius's phrase about the colonists, combined with claims that the Dacian population was annihilated, fed the modern controversy over Daco-Roman continuity and the origins of the Romanians. The gold mines of the Apuseni mountains were exploited by Illyrian (Pirustae) miners brought in for the purpose; the wax tablets from Alburnus Maior (Roșia Montană), dating from 131 to 167, preserve their labour contracts and sales. The province was abandoned by Aurelian around 271-275.
scholarship: Oltean, Dacia: Landscape, Colonisation and Romanisation (2007)
events.debate: Extent of depopulation and Daco-Roman continuity.

events.title: Trajan's Dacian triumph and the games of 107
events.summary: To celebrate the conquest Trajan gave games lasting 123 days, in which, according to Dio, some 11,000 animals were killed and 10,000 gladiators fought. In the same year he called in worn old coins and reissued 'restored' types of Republican and earlier imperial coinage.
events.detail: Dacian booty financed the Forum of Trajan, the baths on the Esquiline and other works; some scholars link a fall in the price of gold to the influx. The silver content of the denarius was reduced to around 89%. The Fasti Ostienses record further games and a naumachia in 109.

events.title: Pliny's governorship of Bithynia and his letter on the Christians
events.summary: Sent by Trajan as special legate to reform the finances of Bithynia-Pontus, Pliny the Younger consulted the emperor on everything from aqueducts to fire brigades. His letter on Christians (Ep. 10.96) and Trajan's reply (10.97) are the earliest surviving official documents on the treatment of Christianity.
events.detail: Pliny executed those who persisted after being asked three times if they were Christians, 'whatever it was they professed, their stubbornness deserved punishment', released those who sacrificed and cursed Christ, and tortured two slave women called deaconesses (ministrae), finding only 'a depraved, excessive superstition'. Trajan replied that Christians were not to be sought out, anonymous accusations were not to be admitted ('not in keeping with our age'), but those convicted who refused to sacrifice must be punished. The same correspondence shows Trajan refusing a fire brigade of 150 men at Nicomedia lest it become a political club.
scholarship: Sherwin-White, The Letters of Pliny: A Historical and Social Commentary (1966)
events.debate: Exact dates of the governorship (109-111 or 110-112).

events.title: Dedication of the Forum of Trajan
events.summary: Trajan dedicated the largest and last of the imperial fora, designed by Apollodorus of Damascus and paid for 'ex manubiis' from the Dacian spoils. It comprised a vast colonnaded square with a gilded equestrian statue of the emperor, the Basilica Ulpia, Greek and Latin libraries and the Column.
events.detail: Building it required cutting away the saddle between the Capitoline and Quirinal; the Markets of Trajan on the Quirinal slope date from the same project. Ammianus records the awe of Constantius II on seeing it in 357, despairing of imitating anything but the horse. The Fasti Ostienses give the date of the Basilica Ulpia's dedication.
scholarship: Packer, The Forum of Trajan in Rome (1997)

events.title: Dedication of Trajan's Column
events.summary: The marble column in Trajan's Forum, 100 Roman feet high on its pedestal, carries a spiral frieze 200 metres long with some 155 scenes and 2,500 figures narrating the Dacian Wars. Trajan's ashes were later placed in its base.
events.detail: Its inscription says it was erected to show how high a hill had been removed for the forum. An internal spiral staircase of 185 steps lit by slits reaches the summit, where Trajan's statue was replaced by St Peter in 1587. The frieze emphasises logistics, building, sacrifice and the emperor's role far more than battle. Scholars debate whether it reflects Trajan's lost Dacica or the work of an artist who never saw Dacia, and how much viewers could actually see.
scholarship: Lepper and Frere, Trajan's Column (1988)
Settis (ed.), La Colonna Traiana (1988)
Coarelli, The Column of Trajan (2000)

events.title: Trajan annexes Armenia
events.summary: When the Parthian king Osroes replaced the Roman-approved king of Armenia with his nephew Parthamasiris, Trajan marched east. At Elegeia Parthamasiris laid his diadem at Trajan's feet expecting it back; Trajan instead declared Armenia a Roman province, and Parthamasiris was killed soon after on the road.
events.detail: The Senate voted Trajan the title Optimus, formalising an epithet used for years. Fronto and Dio criticised the treatment of Parthamasiris as a breach of faith. The annexation broke the Rhandeia compromise that had kept the peace for fifty years.

events.title: Earthquake at Antioch
events.summary: A devastating earthquake struck Antioch, crowded with soldiers and visitors for Trajan's winter court. Trajan escaped through a window with minor injuries, guided, Dio says, by a figure of superhuman size; the consul Marcus Pedo Vergilianus was among the dead.
events.detail: Dio describes survivors buried for days living on milk from a mother's breast. Malalas gives the date. Trajan dedicated a temple to Zeus Kasios on Mount Casius in thanks. Reconstruction was ordered on a large scale.

events.title: Jewish revolts in Cyrene, Egypt and Cyprus
events.summary: While Trajan fought in Parthia, Jews in Cyrenaica rose under Lukuas (Andreas), destroying temples and public buildings; the revolt spread to Egypt and Cyprus with great slaughter on both sides. Dio gives 220,000 killed in Cyrene and 240,000 in Cyprus.
events.detail: Inscriptions at Cyrene record Hadrianic restoration of the baths, temple of Apollo and roads 'torn up and destroyed in the Jewish tumult'. Papyri from Egypt include letters to the strategos Apollonios from his mother and wife fearing for his life. Quintus Marcius Turbo crushed the Egyptian and Cyrenaican risings; Jews were afterwards forbidden to set foot on Cyprus. The Alexandrian community, once the largest in the diaspora, never recovered.
scholarship: Pucci Ben Zeev, Diaspora Judaism in Turmoil, 116/117 CE (2005)

events.title: Trajan captures Ctesiphon
events.summary: Trajan descended the Euphrates with a fleet built from the forests of Nisibis, hauled it overland to the Tigris and took the Parthian winter capital Ctesiphon, capturing Osroes's daughter and golden throne. The Senate voted him the title Parthicus.
events.detail: Osroes fled east. Trajan then sailed down to Charax and the Persian Gulf, where Dio says he watched a ship departing for India and lamented that he was too old to follow Alexander. The Fasti Ostienses date the announcement of the Parthicus title to February 116, which complicates the chronology of the campaigns.

sides.losses: capital and royal family members captured

battle.significance: First capture of the Parthian capital by Rome, the high-water mark of Roman eastward expansion.

events.title: Provinces of Mesopotamia and Assyria; crowning of Parthamaspates
events.summary: Trajan organised his conquests as provinces of Mesopotamia and (according to Eutropius and Festus) Assyria. When revolts broke out across them in 116, he crowned the Parthian prince Parthamaspates king at Ctesiphon, effectively conceding that southern Mesopotamia could not be held.
events.detail: Seleucia, Nisibis and Edessa rebelled; Maximus Santra was killed; Lusius Quietus retook Nisibis and Edessa and Erucius Clarus and Julius Alexander burned Seleucia. Coins show Trajan crowning Parthamaspates with the legend REX PARTHIS DATVS. Whether 'Assyria' was a real province (perhaps Adiabene) is disputed.
events.debate: Existence and location of the province of Assyria.

events.title: Siege of Hatra (117)
events.summary: Trajan attacked the desert caravan city of Hatra, but its walls, the lack of water, wood and fodder, swarms of flies and violent storms defeated him; a cavalryman beside the emperor was killed by an arrow. He withdrew, already ill.
events.detail: Dio notes that the sun-god protected the city, and that Septimius Severus would fail there again (198-199). Hatra's great temple complex and Aramaic inscriptions survive, though damaged by the Islamic State in 2015.

sides.losses: considerable, including from disease and heat

battle.significance: Final failure of Trajan's eastern campaign.

events.title: Death of Trajan
events.summary: On his way back to Rome Trajan suffered a stroke and dropsy and died at Selinus in Cilicia, aged 63. His widow Plotina and the prefect Attianus announced that he had adopted Hadrian on his deathbed.
events.detail: Dio, citing his father Apronianus (later governor of Cilicia), reports a rumour that Plotina concealed the death for days and had someone impersonate Trajan's feeble voice to proclaim the adoption. Selinus was renamed Traianopolis. Trajan's ashes were placed in a golden urn in the base of his Column, an unprecedented burial within the city. Later emperors were acclaimed 'felicior Augusto, melior Traiano' (luckier than Augustus, better than Trajan).

events.title: Accession of Hadrian; abandonment of Trajan's eastern conquests
events.summary: Proclaimed by the Syrian army at Antioch on 11 August 117, Hadrian immediately gave up Mesopotamia and Assyria, restored Armenia to client status, and set Parthamaspates over a smaller kingdom, returning to a frontier on the Euphrates.
events.detail: The Historia Augusta claims he justified this by Cato's dictum that Macedonia should be freed because it could not be held, and that he even considered abandoning Dacia, dissuaded by the fate of the colonists. The removal of the superstructure of Trajan's Danube bridge was ascribed to the same defensive policy. Hostile sources attribute the retreat to jealousy of Trajan's glory; strategically it recognised the impossibility of holding Babylonia.

events.title: Execution of the four consulars
events.summary: Before Hadrian reached Rome, four senior ex-consuls, Lusius Quietus, Cornelius Palma, Avidius Nigrinus and Publilius Celsus, were executed by order of the Senate for an alleged plot. Hadrian claimed he had not ordered it, blamed the prefect Attianus, and swore never to execute a senator without a senatorial trial.
events.detail: All four were Trajanic marshals or potential rivals; Nigrinus may have been an alternative heir. The affair poisoned Hadrian's relations with the Senate for his whole reign. He tried to repair the damage with a donative, the remission of debts and gladiatorial shows.

events.title: Hadrian cancels 900 million sesterces of debts
events.summary: Hadrian remitted 900 million sesterces of arrears owed to the imperial treasury from the preceding sixteen years and had the records publicly burned in the Forum of Trajan.
events.detail: Coins proclaim RELIQVA VETERA HS NOVIES MILL(ies) ABOLITA, and an inscription of the Senate and people (ILS 309) thanks him as the first emperor to free citizens and their descendants from such debts. The reliefs known as the Anaglypha Traiani in the Curia, which show tablets being burned, may depict this or a similar act of Trajan. Hadrian also ordered periodic reviews of debts every fifteen years.

events.title: Rebuilding of the Pantheon
events.summary: Hadrian's Pantheon, with its unreinforced concrete dome 43.3 m in diameter, the same as its height, and an oculus 8.9 m wide, remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Hadrian kept Agrippa's dedicatory inscription on the porch.
events.detail: The concrete aggregate grades from heavy basalt in the foundations to light pumice near the oculus, and the coffering reduces weight further. Brick stamps, mostly from about 115-123, suggest the project was begun in Trajan's last years, possibly to a design by Apollodorus, and completed under Hadrian. The building survived because it was consecrated as the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres in 609; Raphael and two kings of Italy are buried there. The porch columns are monoliths of Egyptian granite.
scholarship: Hetland, 'Dating the Pantheon', JRA 20 (2007)
Wilson Jones, Principles of Roman Architecture (2000)
events.debate: Whether design and construction began under Trajan.

events.title: Hadrian's first great journey
events.summary: Hadrian left Rome in 121 on the first of his tours of the provinces, inspecting armies and cities in Gaul, the German frontier (where he had a continuous palisade of great stakes built), Britain, Spain, Mauretania, the East (averting a Parthian war by a meeting with Osroes), Asia, Greece (initiation at Eleusis) and Sicily (climbing Etna), returning in 125.
events.detail: Hadrian spent more than half his reign outside Italy, governing as a travelling emperor accompanied by architects, engineers and builders organised like a legion. Coin series celebrate provinces, armies (EXERCITVS) and his 'arrivals' (ADVENTVS). He enforced discipline personally, sleeping in the open and marching 20 miles in armour. A second journey (128-132) took him to Africa, Greece, Asia, Syria, Arabia, Judaea and Egypt.
events.locName: Upper German limes and the provinces
scholarship: Birley, Hadrian: The Restless Emperor (1997)
Halfmann, Itinera principum (1986)

events.title: Construction of Hadrian's Wall begins
events.summary: After Hadrian's visit to Britain in 122, the governor Aulus Platorius Nepos began a wall 80 Roman miles long from the Tyne to the Solway, 'to separate the barbarians from the Romans', as the Historia Augusta puts it. It was built by the three British legions, in stone in the east and initially turf in the west.
events.detail: The original plan had milecastles every Roman mile and two turrets between each, with forts behind on the Stanegate; within a few years forts were added on the line, and the Vallum, a great ditch with mounds, was dug to the south marking a military zone. Building inscriptions of legions II Augusta, VI Victrix and XX Valeria Victrix survive. Souvenir enamelled pans (the Rudge Cup, the Staffordshire Moorlands Pan) list forts on the wall. Its function, defensive barrier or controlled frontier for customs and policing, is debated.
scholarship: Breeze and Dobson, Hadrian's Wall (4th ed. 2000)
Hodgson, Hadrian's Wall: Archaeology and History at the Limit of Rome's Empire (2017)

events.title: Hadrian's address to the army at Lambaesis
events.summary: After watching manoeuvres of legio III Augusta and its auxiliaries in Numidia, Hadrian addressed the troops, and his speeches were inscribed on a column base at Lambaesis. They are the only surviving texts of an emperor's adlocutio to soldiers.
events.detail: The emperor's remarks are specific and technical: he praises a cohort for building a wall in less time than usual, notes that the legion was understrength because a cohort had been sent to help another province and men transferred, criticises cavalry for chasing too fast, and commends the legate Quintus Fabius Catullinus. The inscriptions (CIL VIII 2532 and 18042) show Hadrian's hands-on style of command.
scholarship: Speidel, Emperor Hadrian's Speeches to the African Army: A New Text (2006)

events.title: Death of Antinous
events.summary: Hadrian's young Bithynian favourite Antinous drowned in the Nile near Hermopolis during the imperial tour of Egypt. Hadrian wept 'like a woman', founded the city of Antinoopolis at the spot on 30 October 130, and promoted the cult of Antinous as a god throughout the Greek East.
events.detail: Dio reports that Hadrian claimed it was an accident but others said Antinous sacrificed himself to prolong the emperor's life. Over a hundred portrait statues survive, more than of almost any other ancient figure apart from emperors, as well as coins struck by Greek cities, and Hadrian named a star after him. The obelisk now on the Pincian carries hieroglyphs describing his deification.
scholarship: Lambert, Beloved and God (1984)
Vout, Power and Eroticism in Imperial Rome (2007)

events.title: Foundation of Aelia Capitolina
events.summary: During his visit to Judaea in 130 Hadrian refounded the ruins of Jerusalem as a Roman colony, Colonia Aelia Capitolina, named after his family and Jupiter Capitolinus, with a temple to Jupiter on or near the Temple site. Dio names this as the cause of the Bar Kokhba revolt.
events.detail: Coins of Aelia showing the founding ritual of ploughing the boundary have been found in hoards together with Bar Kokhba coins, supporting a foundation before the revolt. The Historia Augusta gives a different cause, a ban on circumcision. After 135 Jews were forbidden to enter the city except, according to later tradition, on the 9th of Av. The city's Roman plan (the cardo, the Damascus Gate) underlies the Old City today.
events.debate: Whether the colony was founded before or after the revolt; relative weight of the colony and the circumcision ban as causes.

events.title: Codification of the praetor's edict
events.summary: On Hadrian's orders the jurist Salvius Julianus revised and fixed the text of the edict issued by the urban praetor (and the aediles' edict), which had grown by annual accretion since the Republic. Thereafter only the emperor could change it.
events.detail: The 'perpetual edict' ended the praetor's creative role in Roman law, shifting legal innovation to imperial constitutions and juristic interpretation. Its text, lost as such, was reconstructed by Otto Lenel (1883) from commentaries quoted in Justinian's Digest. Julianus, a North African from Hadrumetum, held a double salary as quaestor for his learning and became one of the most cited jurists.
scholarship: Lenel, Das Edictum Perpetuum (1883; 3rd ed. 1927)

events.title: Dedication of the Olympieion and foundation of the Panhellenion
events.summary: Hadrian completed the colossal temple of Olympian Zeus at Athens, begun under Peisistratos six centuries earlier, and founded the Panhellenion, a league of Greek cities of proven Hellenic descent with its seat at Athens.
events.detail: Member cities from Achaea, Macedonia, Thrace, Asia, Crete and Cyrene sent delegates; Hadrian was honoured as Panhellenios and Olympios. The Arch of Hadrian bears inscriptions on its two faces: 'This is Athens, the ancient city of Theseus' and 'This is the city of Hadrian and not of Theseus'. Pausanias describes the chryselephantine cult statue and the many statues of Hadrian dedicated by cities.
scholarship: Spawforth and Walker, 'The world of the Panhellenion', JRS 75-76 (1985-86)

events.title: Outbreak of the Bar Kokhba revolt
events.summary: Soon after Hadrian left the East, the Jews of Judaea rose under Simon bar Kosiba, whom Rabbi Akiva hailed as the messianic 'son of the star'. Prepared in secret, with weapons deliberately made defective for the Romans and then kept, the rebels operated from underground hideouts and drove the Romans from much of Judaea.
events.detail: Dio's account of underground tunnels with air shafts is confirmed by hundreds of hiding complexes in the Judaean foothills. The rebel state minted silver and bronze by overstriking Roman coins with legends such as 'Year One of the redemption of Israel', 'Simon prince of Israel', and the Temple facade, and issued land leases. Letters of Bar Kosiba himself, found in the Judaean desert caves in 1951-61, show a harsh commander concerned with supplies and the observance of Sukkot. The governor Tineius Rufus was overwhelmed and legions from Syria, Egypt and beyond were sent.
scholarship: Eshel, 'The Bar Kochba Revolt, 132-135', in Cambridge History of Judaism IV (2006)
Schäfer (ed.), The Bar Kokhba War Reconsidered (2003)

events.title: Arrian repels the Alans from Cappadocia
events.summary: When the nomadic Alans, encouraged by king Pharasmanes of Iberia, broke through the Caucasus and raided Media and Armenia, the governor of Cappadocia, the historian Flavius Arrianus, mustered legions XV Apollinaris and XII Fulminata with auxiliaries and deterred them from invading the province.
events.detail: Arrian's 'Order of Battle against the Alans' (Ektaxis kata Alanon) survives in part, describing marching order and a defensive formation of legionaries with long pikes in eight ranks, archers and artillery behind, designed to break a heavy cavalry charge. It is the only surviving battle plan by a Roman commander. Arrian also wrote a Periplus of the Black Sea for Hadrian, the Anabasis of Alexander, and recorded Epictetus's Discourses.
scholarship: Bosworth, 'Arrian and the Alani', HSCP 81 (1977)

events.title: Siege of Betar
events.summary: Sextus Julius Severus, brought from Britain, ground down the revolt by attacking small groups and starving them out. The last stronghold, Betar, a hill town south-west of Jerusalem, fell after a long siege; Bar Kosiba was killed.
events.detail: Eusebius says the defenders perished from hunger and thirst. Rabbinic tradition dates the fall to the 9th of Av, the same day as the destructions of both Temples, and tells of rivers of blood. Remains of the Roman siege wall and camps survive around Khirbet el-Yahud near Battir. Hadrian and his generals received triumphal honours but Hadrian did not celebrate a triumph.

sides.strength: Legions X Fretensis, VI Ferrata and detachments from many others
sides.losses: unknown; Dio says many Romans died in the war

battle.significance: Ended organised Jewish resistance; final end of Jewish political independence in antiquity.

events.title: Temple of Venus and Roma
events.summary: Hadrian dedicated the largest temple in Rome, designed by himself, on the Velia between the Forum and the Colosseum, with back-to-back cellae for Venus Felix and Roma Aeterna; it was completed under Antoninus Pius.
events.detail: Dio tells that Apollodorus criticised the design, saying the seated goddesses were too tall for their cellae and would hit their heads if they stood up, and that Hadrian, already offended by an earlier jibe ('go and draw your pumpkins'), exiled and later executed him. Many historians doubt the story. The temple's date (dedication in 135 or 136/137) is uncertain; the Natalis Urbis (21 April) was celebrated there as the Romaia.

events.title: Judaea renamed Syria Palaestina
events.summary: After the revolt the province of Judaea was renamed Syria Palaestina, erasing the name of the Jews from the map, and Jews were banned from Jerusalem. Dio records that Judaea was left almost desolate.
events.detail: The name first appears in a military diploma of 139. Rabbinic tradition remembers the 'decrees of persecution' (gezerot) against Torah study and circumcision, and the martyrdom of Rabbi Akiva and other sages; Antoninus Pius later exempted Jews from the ban on circumcision. The rabbinic centre moved to Galilee (Usha, later Sepphoris and Tiberias), where the Mishnah was compiled c. 200.

events.title: Hadrian's Villa at Tibur
events.summary: Below Tibur Hadrian built a palace-villa covering some 120 hectares, a summary of the empire with buildings named, according to the Historia Augusta, after famous places: the Lyceum, the Academy, the Prytaneum, the Canopus, the Poikile and the Vale of Tempe.
events.detail: Innovative domed and curvilinear spaces, such as the Maritime Theatre (an island retreat ringed by a moat) and the Piazza d'Oro, show architectural experimentation probably by the emperor himself. The villa's statuary, including copies of the Erechtheion caryatids around the Canopus pool and images of Antinous, has filled museums since the Renaissance. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
scholarship: MacDonald and Pinto, Hadrian's Villa and Its Legacy (1995)

events.title: Hadrian's succession arrangements
events.summary: In 136 Hadrian adopted Lucius Ceionius Commodus as Lucius Aelius Caesar and forced his 90-year-old brother-in-law Servianus and Servianus's grandson Pedanius Fuscus to die. When Aelius died on 1 January 138, Hadrian adopted Titus Aurelius Antoninus on 25 February 138, on condition that Antoninus adopt both the young Marcus Annius Verus (the future Marcus Aurelius) and Aelius's son Lucius.
events.detail: Servianus, before dying, prayed that Hadrian might long for death and be unable to die. The double adoption laid down the succession for two generations and reveals Hadrian's interest in Marcus, whom he nicknamed Verissimus. Some scholars think Antoninus was meant only as a placeholder for Marcus.

events.title: Death of Hadrian
events.summary: After a long, painful illness during which he repeatedly begged for poison or a sword, Hadrian died at Baiae aged 62. The Historia Augusta preserves the poem he is said to have composed on his deathbed, beginning 'animula vagula blandula' ('little soul, wandering, charming').
events.detail: He was first buried at Puteoli; his ashes were moved to the great Mausoleum across the Tiber (now Castel Sant'Angelo), completed by Antoninus in 139. The Senate, resentful, was reluctant to deify him; Antoninus insisted, and received the name Pius, perhaps for this act of filial devotion. Marguerite Yourcenar's novel Memoirs of Hadrian (1951) shaped his modern image.
